idiom_name: ACE_TP_Reactor (thread pool reactor) over the ACE Reactor; TAO_Leader_Follower for ORB upcalls
implementation_notes: C++ ships this pattern as framework code: ACE's ACE_TP_Reactor is documented as the "thread pool reactor" that "uses the Leader/Followers pattern to demultiplex events among a pool of threads" - a fixed, pre-spawned pool in which each thread calling handle_events() competes for an internal token, one becomes the leader, and before each upcall the activated handler is suspended while the reactor lock is released so that another thread can start waiting. TAO's TAO_Leader_Follower applies the same machinery to ORB threads (follower set, elect_new_leader(), reverse lock, deferred events). Two caveats are documented: the suspend/resume protection covers I/O upcalls only - timers and notifications are not suspended, so handlers reached that way must protect themselves - and the reactor's owner() reports the current leader rather than a fixed thread. The modern alternative is running a Boost.Asio io_context on a fixed thread pool: Asio declares all pool threads equivalent and distributes work across them arbitrarily, which is the same shape with the promotion protocol moved inside the library.
pitfalls: ACE_TP_Reactor suspends only the activated I/O handler; timers and notifications are dispatched without that protection, so their handlers run concurrently and need their own locking.
The reactor's owner() is the current leader, not a stable thread - caching it or assuming thread affinity of the pool breaks.
Calling handle_events() re-entrantly from a handler consumes the leader role and stalls the pool; long-running callbacks are supported, but they must not wait for new events.
A single reactor token means one slow upcall delays the next leader's readiness evaluation, so latency-sensitive handlers must stay short or be moved off the reactor thread.
